You are an independent classifier in a blinded experiment about a book of
biblical symbolism. The consensus responses below were produced without access
to the book. Compare them with the book's entry.

TERM
Way (the way)

BLIND CONSENSUS RESPONSES
RESPONSE A
{
  "primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching, 'the Way' primarily symbolizes Jesus Christ himself as the sole path or means of access to God the Father — salvation understood not as a technique or map but as a person to be followed. By extension it denotes the whole life of discipleship: following Jesus is walking 'the way' to God.",
  "primary_basis": [
    "John 14:6 ('I am the way, and the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me')",
    "John 14:4-5 (Thomas's question about the way)",
    "Hebrews 10:19-20 ('a new and living way' opened through Christ's flesh)",
    "Matthew 7:13-14 (the narrow way that leads to life)",
    "Isaiah 40:3 / Matthew 3:3 / Mark 1:2-3 / Luke 3:4 ('prepare the way of the Lord,' applied to Jesus)",
    "John 10:9 and Acts 4:12 (often cited alongside as expressing exclusive access through Christ)"
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "'The Way' as the earliest self-designation or name for the Christian movement itself — the community of Jesus-followers before the label 'Christian' became standard. This is treated as historical fact in scholarship and is frequently folded into the primary christological reading (the movement was named for following Jesus who is the way).",
      "basis": [
        "Acts 9:2",
        "Acts 19:9, 19:23",
        "Acts 22:4",
        "Acts 24:14, 24:22"
      ],
      "prominence": "dominant"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "The 'two ways' moral tradition: 'way' as a manner of life or moral path — the way of the righteous versus the way of the wicked — an ethical rather than strictly christological symbol, prominent in Old Testament wisdom literature and early Christian catechesis.",
      "basis": [
        "Psalm 1:1-6",
        "Proverbs 4:18-19; 12:28",
        "Deuteronomy 30:15-19",
        "Jeremiah 21:8",
        "Matthew 7:13-14",
        "Didache 1:1 (extra-biblical but widely cited in scholarship)"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "The 'way of the Lord' as God's own conduct, commandments, or Torah — walking in God's ways as covenant obedience; in Christian appropriation this Old Testament usage is often read as background or type fulfilled in Christ.",
      "basis": [
        "Genesis 18:19",
        "Deuteronomy 8:6; 10:12",
        "Psalm 119:1, 119:32-33",
        "Isaiah 55:8-9",
        "Exodus 33:13"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "The eschatological highway of return from exile: Isaiah's prepared way through the wilderness as the path of God's redemptive return, read by some scholars (e.g., in studies of Mark's 'way' motif) as the controlling image behind New Testament 'way' language — a new-exodus journey motif rather than simply a metaphor for Jesus.",
      "basis": [
        "Isaiah 40:3-5",
        "Isaiah 35:8-10 (the Highway of Holiness)",
        "Isaiah 43:16-19",
        "Mark 1:2-3 with Mark's repeated 'on the way' framing (Mark 8:27; 9:33-34; 10:32, 10:52)"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "The way as mystical or ascetic ascent — the spiritual journey or pilgrimage of the soul toward God (via purgativa/illuminativa/unitiva in later spiritual theology), using biblical 'way' texts as launching points for interior progress.",
      "basis": [
        "Psalm 84:5 ('in whose heart are the highways to Zion')",
        "John 14:6 as read in mystical tradition",
        "Hebrews 11:13-16 (pilgrim motif)"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "There is a strong, recognizable consensus: 'the Way' in Christian symbolism centers on John 14:6 — Christ as the exclusive way to the Father — combined with the Acts usage naming the earliest Christian movement 'the Way.' These two strands are usually presented together rather than as rivals. The main interpretive variation concerns emphasis: christological/person-centered (dominant), ethical two-ways lifestyle (common), covenantal Old Testament walking in God's ways (common as background), and the Isaianic new-exodus reading favored in some modern academic work (minority). This assessment is made without knowledge of the author's book or argument."
}

BOOK ENTRY
Covenant conduct — the walk.

BOOK'S COMMON-VIEW NOTE, IF PRESENT
Commonly taught: Jesus Himself as the one way to the Father; the narrow way against the broad.

SCRIPTURE REFERENCES PRINTED WITH THE ENTRY
(Jer 6:16; Matt 7:14) · see The Way, the Truth & the Life, ch. 7

AVAILABLE KJV EXCERPTS
Jeremiah 6:16 — Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein.
Matthew 7:14 — Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it.

CLASSIFY THE RELATIONSHIP

First reduce both readings to their minimum core identifications. Do not let
extra detail create an artificial disagreement.

- MATCH: the core identifications are equivalent. Differences are merely
  wording or immaterial detail.
- REFINED: the book preserves the consensus's general referent or category but
  materially changes its extension, boundary, conditions, or precision. A
  narrowing may reject some cases the broader consensus admits; a broadening
  may admit cases it excludes. This is real disagreement at the boundary, but
  not replacement of the central referent.
- DIVERGENT: the cores materially contradict. Both claims cannot be true of the
  same referent in the same context and sense; accepting the book requires
  rejecting or replacing the consensus identification. A source and its
  product remain different referents when the book explicitly denies their
  identity, even if they are causally related.
- NOVEL: no recognizable consensus or listed alternative covers the book's
  core identification. Novelty is absence from consensus, not contradiction.

Use `core_relation` to expose the relationship at the center and
`extension_relation` to expose disagreement over the cases covered. A REFINED
verdict must state what cases the book adds, excludes, or reclassifies. A
DIVERGENT verdict must identify a replaced referent or material contradiction,
not merely a narrower boundary.

Treat the two axes independently. A core-divergent reading may still retain
some cases covered by the consensus while rejecting its central identification;
therefore DIVERGENT does not require disjoint extensions. Conversely, a
narrowed extension is REFINED only when the consensus's central referent or
category remains intact.

Also judge whether the citations printed with the glossary entry alone provide
strong, partial, or insufficient support. Do not yet decide whether a divergent
full chapter is persuasive; that is a separate stage.
